item.title: Population models
item.description:
Population models

In this chapter we discuss models for populations data. Those data contain observations from a set of individuals sampled from a population. Such data are characterized by one or more observations for each individual. All the models discussed here are parameter models, in that observations are described with models with parameters. These models are capable of explaining the data variability due to the those unknown random parameters.

item.title: PK and ODEs
item.description:
Pharmacokinetics and ordinary differential equations

Since pharmacokinetics (PK) always involves time \(t\), we make it explicit in the population data formulation from the last chapter. To simplify notation we also assume homoscedasticity and hide the subscripts for the moment: $$ y = f(x, \phi, t) + \epsilon. $$ In general the \(x\), \(y\), \(\phi\), and \(\epsilon\) are vectors.

For example, let us consider \(x=D\), \(D\) being the single bolus dose amount, and \(\theta=(V, k)\) with \(V\) for the volumne of distribution and \(k\) the elminination coefficient, in one-compartment models. For the plasma concentration observation \(y\), we have $$ y=\frac{D}{V}e^{-kt} +\epsilon, $$ thus the canonical form of \(f\) is $$ F=f(D, (V, k), t)=\frac{D}{V}e^{-kt} $$

item.title: Likelihood and MLE
item.description:
Likelihood and MLE

To summarize the previous two chapters, in NONMEM nomenclature, a model consists of a structure component $$ y = f(x, \phi, t) + \epsilon, $$ and a statistical component $$ \phi = \mu(z, \theta, \eta). $$ Another formulation is through the likelihood. Let \(p(y_i|\phi_i, \Sigma_i)\) be the likelihood function for individual i, as a function of the individual parameter \(\phi_i\) and residual covariance matrix \(\Sigma_i\). Then NONMEM's assumption that observation \(y_i\) follows a multivariate normal distribution can be expressed as $$ p(y_i|\phi_i, \Sigma_i) \propto \det(\Sigma_i)^{1/2}\exp\left[ -\frac{1}{2}(y_i-f(x, \phi_i, t))^T\Sigma_i^{-1}(y_i-f(x, \phi_i, t)) \right]. $$ Assume \(\phi_i=\mu(z_i, \theta)+\eta_i\) and recall that \(\eta_i\) also has multivariate normal distribution: $$ p(\phi_i | \theta, \Omega) \propto \det(\Omega)^{1/2}\exp\left[ -\frac{1}{2}\eta_i^T\Omega\eta_i \right], $$ then the individual likelihood is $$ p(y_i|\eta_i, \Sigma_i, \theta, \Omega)=p(y_i|\phi_i, \Sigma_i)p(\phi_i | \theta, \Omega). $$ In classical NONMEM methods, we only seek the likelihood of population parameters by marginalizing \(\eta_i\), so that the individual likelihood of the population parameters is $$ L_i\equiv p(y_i|\Sigma_i, \theta, \Omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(y_i|\phi_i, \Sigma_i)p(\phi_i | \theta, \Omega)\,d\phi_i = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(y_i|\phi_i, \Sigma_i)p(\eta_i | \Omega)\,d\eta_i, $$ The total likelihood for the population is $$ L=\Pi_iL_i=L_1\times L_2\times\dots \times L_{N}. $$ The reason that we use "proportional to" (\(\propto\)) instead of "equal to" (\(=\)) is that we fit the model by maximizing the likelihood L, and the normalizing coefficients are not relevant. In fact, we maximize the log-likelihood \(\mathcal{L}\) for its superior numerical statbility and being simpler to work with for common distributions (from the expontential family): $$ \mathcal{L}=\sum_i\mathcal{L}_i=\sum_i\log(L_i). $$ NONMEM's point estimating methods aim to adjust parameters to maximize \(\mathcal{L}\). These methods are called maximized likelihood estimations (MLEs), and the corresponding "optimal" parameter values maximized likelihood estimates, denoted as \(\hat{\theta}\), \(\hat{\Omega}\), and \(\hat{\Sigma}\). In fact, NONMEM takes one step further by minimizing certain approximations of \(-2\mathcal{L}\), and call these approximations objective function \(\mathcal{T}\) and objective function for individual \(\mathcal{T}_i\). Though different NONMEM MLE methods define \(\mathcal{T}\) differently, they all aim to simplify \(\mathcal{L}\) evaluation while keep the minimizer "close" to the MLE solution: $$ \text{arg}\,\text{min}_{\theta, \Omega, \Sigma}\,\mathcal{T}\approx \text{arg}\,\text{min}_{\theta, \Omega, \Sigma}\,\mathcal{-2L}=\text{arg}\,\text{max}_{\theta, \Omega, \Sigma}\,\mathcal{L}. $$ The approximation is unbiased in predicted individual mean responses. These predictions are obtained setting \(\hat{\eta}=0\) and \(\epsilon=0\). In other words, the prediction is for the mean reponses of individuals with same fixed effects. In addition, one can also use \(\hat{\theta}\), \(\hat{\Omega}\), and \(\hat{\Sigma}\) to calculate the covariance matrix (hence the standard error) of individual predictions.
